newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Court setback for Argentine telecoms in rates war.
newsitem.headline: Court setback for Argentine telecoms in rates war.

text.p: A federal judge Friday snatched victory from Argentina's two near-monopolistic telephone companies in their long campaign to restructure call rates, suspending the government's approval of the move.
Shares in Telefonica de Argentina and Telecom de Argentina surged last week after the decree authorizing the tariff changes.

But Judge Maria Jose Sarmiento poured cold water on the euphoria, suspending the decree until a there is a ruling on a court case to have the tariff changes reversed which was lodged by the nation's Ombudsman.

Sarmiento ruled that the decree was not approved by a public hearing last December and so was issued in defiance of previous court orders. She said this meant the Ombudsman's legal action was worthy of consideration.

"Such a circumstance, without need of further consideration, is more than sufficient to justify ... the necessary grounds to lodge measures such as that which has been solicited (by the Ombudsman)," the judge ruled.

Telecom is controlled by France Telecom and Telefonica by Telefonica de Espana. The government granted them each near monopolies in territories which divided up Argentina between them when the former state telephone company ENTEL was privatized in 1990.

The call rate changes approved by the government decree abolished free local call time, boosted the price of other local calls, and increased monthly rental charges. But the cost of the longest distance domestic calls fell by 56 percent and international call rates to major destinations were cut by an average of 42 percent.

Ombudsman Jorge Maiorano, who is appointed by Congress to defend the rights of common citizens, greeted the decision with cautious optimism and said that the chances of final success had been increased by other court cases lodged in recent days against the rates restructuring.
"I think this generates short-term incertitude, but no one doubts that in the long term the price restructuring will go through," he said.

He described as fallacious the argument that the tariff restructuring violates the terms of the 1990 telephone privatization, and said that support from the provinces for cheaper long-distance rates will eventually weigh heavily.
"As an investor, as a fund manager, I would not sell Telefonica just on this news," Galvan declared.
Telecom and Telefonica stocks were not much affected by the latest move, but fell earlier in the week when the Ombudsman launched his court action.

Telefonica and Telecom had waged a long lobbying compaign for the tariff changes, which they said would make charges fairer for business in the provinces. They also hoped it would make them more competitive when the Argentine phone market is thrown open to all competitors, probably in the year 2000.
They also face competition from offshore call-back services offering cheap long-distance calls.

But consumer groups and opposition parties fought hard against the changes, and argued in public hearings ending in December 1996 that private users' telephone bills would rise and the phone companies would pocket the difference.
Telecom stressed that there was "no way the rebalancing would mean higher earnings for the companies."

Provincial business chambers applauded the decree but opposition groups and newspapers in Buenos Aires were furious. Opposition parties proposed organizing a mass boycott of telephones for 15 minutes next week.
"It is a first step, an important step," he said, "Now we are going to press ahead with the court case."
He added "The important thing is to join forces, bring our separate wills together to put a stop to the pretensions of the monopolic companies supported by the decree."
But Sergio Galvn, head of research at private bank Bansud, said that the latest ruling would probably turn out to be nothing more than a short-term nuisance.
